Do not edit files in `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles` directly on `master`. Branch
and work in a worktree, then merge. The user caught me mid-task editing the main
tree and said so bluntly ("why the fuck are you working in the main tree"),
then: "reset main after you fix it".

**Why:** master is the tree `hms` reads, and `hms` refuses on a dirty tree — so
uncommitted edits in the main checkout block applying config, and they sit in the
one place the user expects to be clean. A worktree also keeps the main checkout
usable while work is in progress.

**How to apply:** `git worktree add .drovr/wt/<name> -b <branch> HEAD`, add
`.drovr/wt` to `.git/info/exclude` (not the tracked `.gitignore`), then
`EnterWorktree` into it. Note that master may be **amended** under you while you
work — check `git merge-base --is-ancestor <base> master` before merging, and
replay with `git rebase --onto master <base> <branch>` rather than a plain merge
that would resurrect rewritten commits.

When a change is verified by a harness, the harness belongs in `tests/` in the
commit, not in the session's scratch directory. Asked on 2026-09-27 whether to
commit one (and whether to apply with `hms`), the answer was "always do it" —

comments asserting the model is right are exactly what needs re-checking after an
upstream bump.

evaluates and realises the real artifact and tests that, so it runs with no
setup; a path argument tests a given build. Drive the code through override seams
(env vars) so no real failure state has to be provoked. Mention it in README.

Never treat `git push` as a step that can stand alone in this repo. If the
change is going to origin, run `hms` — it pushes, waits for the commit's CI run
on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches to the closure CI built. Offering "want me to
push?" as separate from switching was the mistake; the user's words: "god damn
if you push you MUST hms".

**Why:** a pushed-but-not-switched master is a half-applied state. CI builds
every pushed commit, so a push already commits the machine to that closure;
stopping before the switch just leaves the box running old config while origin
says otherwise, and the next `hms` then switches to a commit nobody reviewed as
current.

**How to apply:** when work is committed and ready, run `hms` (background it —
it blocks ten-odd minutes). Never propose `git push` on its own, and never
substitute `home-manager switch`. `hms --local` builds here instead of
downloading CI's build, and is a deliberate choice to state out loud.

# dotfiles

Home Manager configuration for `sauyon`.

## New machine setup

For a blank machine (ISO, disk, base Arch install), see
[docs/new-host.md](docs/new-host.md). The steps below assume Arch is already
running.

```bash
# 1. Clone into ~/devel/dotfiles
mkdir -p ~/devel
git clone https://github.com/sauyon/dotfiles ~/devel/dotfiles

# 2. If this is a new host, add a homeConfigurations entry for it in flake.nix
#    (hostname, gui, gpu). Otherwise the matching entry already exists.

# 3. Install Nix
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf -L https://install.determinate.systems/nix \
  | sudo sh -s -- install --no-confirm

# 4. Source Nix and trust mise
. /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh
mise trust ~/devel/dotfiles/mise.toml

# 5. Apply (flake attr matches hostname)
nix run github:nix-community/home-manager -- switch --flake ~/devel/dotfiles#$HOST
```

After the first switch, `home-manager switch` is available directly.

## Applying changes: `hms`

`hms` is the normal way to switch. It does **not** build locally by default — it
pushes, waits for the commit's CI run, then switches, which turns the switch into
a download of the closure the runner already built and pushed to attic.

```bash
hms              # push, wait for the run, then switch
hms --local      # skip CI and build here (the old `home-manager switch` alias)
```

Things it deliberately refuses rather than works around:

- **A dirty tree.** CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch is one CI
  can never reproduce. Commit, or use `--local`.
- **A stale checkout.** If `origin/master` has commits you do not, it says so and
  stops — rebasing is your call, and waiting on a run for a SHA that is not
  `origin/master` would be waiting on the wrong build.

It falls back to a local build, with a note, when the host has no CI job (mari)
or when the commit touched nothing `nix-home.yml`'s `paths:` filter matches. On a
red run it prints the job's actual `error:` lines, not just a status.

Why this is worth a wait: see `docs/ci-nix-home.md`. The short version is that
the runner has far more of everything than these boxes, and its output is
bit-identical to what a local build would produce.

## Tests

Nothing here has a suite; the exception is anything whose logic is a model of
someone else's, where a comment claiming the model is right proves nothing.

```bash
./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh     # builds the script, then drives 33 cases
```

`hyprlock-faillock` (in `home.nix`) reproduces pam_faillock's two tally windows
to tell the lock screen whether the account is locked out. The cases drive the
real built script through its `FAILLOCK_BIN` / `FAILLOCK_CONF` / `FAILLOCK_USER`
seams, so a stub reader supplies synthetic tally records -- no real failed
logins, no waiting out a real ten-minute lockout.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# ── host packages: converge pacman onto ./packages ───────────────────────────
# install-base.sh pacstraps the same list, but that only ever runs on the live
# ISO, so a package added after a host was built never reaches it.
#
# The order against the etc/ copy below does not matter, and it is worth saying
# so rather than inventing a reason: pacman owns NONE of the seven files that
# copy writes (`pacman -Qo` on each answers "No package owns"). Everything under
# etc/ is an override path -- /etc/pam.d/polkit-1 shadows the polkit package's
# /usr/lib/pam.d/polkit-1, /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service shadows the
# packaged unit -- which is the mechanism that makes this whole directory work.
# Nor does the order spare any pam_fprintd load errors: every existing host has
# had that state since the polkit-1 stack was committed, and a fresh host
# pacstraps fprintd before deploy ever runs.
#
# An explicit host list, NOT `command -v pacman`: those are different
# predicates. kyuusaku is a box whose OS we do not own, and an Arch-based one
# would sail through a capability check and be handed a base metapackage.
# docs/new-host.md step 0 says to add a new host here. It happens to be the same
# four hosts as home.nix's `hms` case, but for an unrelated reason (that one
# means "has a Linux CI job"), so do not treat the two as one list -- kyuusaku
# is absent from both for different reasons, and a CI job would earn it a place
# in hms without earning one here.
#
# A host that is not listed still gets the etc/ copy below, so it keeps a
# pam_fprintd line it cannot load -- fail-safe (polkit falls through to the
# password) at the price of a log line per auth.
#
# A failure here WARNS and carries on rather than aborting: nothing later in
# this script is about packages, and the attic netrc further down is what lets
# the home-manager switch after it download CI's closure instead of compiling
# for an hour. Letting a stale mirror take that down would be a worse outcome
# than a host missing fprintd. SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES to any value skips the step
# outright -- tested for non-emptiness, so SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES=0 skips too.
#
# Without --noconfirm this step can PROMPT (pacman's "Proceed with installation?"),
# so a deploy driven over ssh wants a tty. Without one, pacman takes its defaults
# or aborts, and either way the warn-and-continue above keeps the rest running.
#
# `uname -n`, not $HOSTNAME and not hostname(1): the kernel owns it where an env
# var is inheritable, the repo derives the host this way in three other places
# (home.nix's hms, two mise tasks), and hostname(1) lives in inetutils, which is
# installed on none of these boxes.
if [ -n "${SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES:-}" ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES set -- not touching pacman."
else
host=$(uname -n)
case "${host%%.*}" in
utsuho | setsuna | shiori | fujiwara)
  [ -r packages ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages is missing or unreadable" >&2; exit 1; }
  # Strip comments, then split on any whitespace. One package per line is the
  # documented format; splitting rather than deleting whitespace means a
  # two-names-on-one-line slip fails as two packages instead of silently
  # concatenating into one bogus name.
  mapfile -t want < <(sed 's/#.*//' packages | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sed '/^$/d')
  # mapfile returns 0 whatever the process substitution did, and neither `set
  # -e` nor pipefail sees inside one, so an empty parse has to be caught by
  # hand. Without this a renamed or emptied list makes this step a silent
  # no-op -- the exact failure the list was added to fix.
  [ ${#want[@]} -gt 0 ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages parsed to nothing" >&2; exit 1; }

  missing=()
  for p in "${want[@]}"; do
    # -Qq resolves virtual provides (`pacman -Qq sh` answers bash), so an entry
    # satisfied by a provider is not reported missing.
    pacman -Qq -- "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("$p")
  done

  if [ ${#missing[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "system/deploy: installing missing host packages: ${missing[*]}"
    # `--` because the list is data: a line starting with a dash would
    # otherwise be read as a pacman option (--hookdir=, --overwrite=, --root=),
    # and this runs under sudo.
    #
    # No `--noconfirm`, which answers every question with its default -- and the
    # default to "replace X with Y?" is yes. So a line here that reads as purely
    # additive could silently REMOVE a package from a running host by pulling in
    # something that replaces it. (Whether the separate "X conflicts with Y,
    # remove Y?" question also defaults to yes I did not confirm; it does not
    # change the conclusion.) Prompting costs a keypress, and only when something
    # is actually missing.
    #
    # No `-y` either: refreshing the db and then installing without upgrading is
    # the partial-upgrade footgun. `-S` against the db as it stands resolves the
    # version matching the libraries already installed, which is the safe
    # direction. It is not a guarantee -- if the db is already newer than the
    # system because something ran `pacman -Sy` by hand, installing anything
    # here drags its newer deps in and you get a partial upgrade through the
    # other door. Nothing this script can do about that; `-Syu` is the cure.
    #
    # Failure is a warning, not an abort (see the header): a stale db 404, a
    # held pacman lock, a refused sudo password, a full /var, an unresolvable
    # conflict. Any of them, and the rest of the deploy still runs.
    sudo pacman -S --needed -- "${missing[@]}" || {
      echo "system/deploy: pacman failed for: ${missing[*]}" >&2
      echo "  Common causes: a stale sync db (404 on a dropped version -- fix" >&2
      echo "  with 'sudo pacman -Syu'), another pacman holding the db lock, or" >&2
      echo "  no network. Continuing; nothing below needs these packages." >&2
    }
  fi
  ;;
*)
  echo "system/deploy: ${host%%.*} is not one of our Arch hosts -- skipping host packages."
  ;;
esac
fi

questions.question: How should Steam be installed on shiori?

options.label: pacman + multilib (Recommended)
options.description: Uncomment [multilib] in /etc/pacman.conf, then add steam + lib32-mesa + lib32-vulkan-intel to system/packages. Native, standard Arch path, best GPU support on Panther Lake. Cost: a root config file the repo doesn't manage gets hand-edited (I'd note it in docs/ or overlay pacman.conf).

options.label: Flatpak
options.description: Add flatpak to system/packages and install com.valvesoftware.Steam. No multilib needed — the runtime ships its own 32-bit stack and mesa. Cost: a second package manager, sandbox friction (controllers, ~/ paths, external drives).

options.description: pkgs.steam in home.nix wrapped with nixGL. Stays in the declarative config. Cost: steam's FHS env on non-NixOS needs 32-bit GL that nixGLIntel doesn't reliably provide — most likely to end in a debugging spiral.

options.label: All GUI Arch hosts

options.description: system/deploy seds the two commented [multilib] lines live if it finds them commented. No new files, but it's an in-place edit of someone else's config and the desired state lives in bash, not in a file.

# TDD

## Overview

**Test-first, always.** Write the failing test before the code it covers, watch
it fail, then write the minimal code to make it pass. A test you never saw fail
proves nothing — it may pass for the wrong reason, or not exercise the behavior
at all.

Keep the test scoped to the interfaces you are actually changing — a test that
drifts wider stops being a contract anyone can rely on. Inside a drovr phase
this also binds the next phase's contract.

## The cycle

1. **RED** — write the failing test named in the task's verification. Run it.
   *Watch it fail*, and confirm it fails for the reason you expect (missing
   behavior, not a typo or compile error elsewhere).
2. **GREEN** — write the *minimal* code to make that test pass. No extra
   features, no speculative abstraction — just enough to go green.
3. **REFACTOR** — clean up with the test as your safety net, re-running it.

Repeat per behavior. One failing test at a time.

## Red flags — STOP

- Wrote code before the test → delete it, start with the test.
- "I'll add the test after" → tests-after check *what the code does*, not what it
  *should* do. Test first.
- Test passed the first time you ran it → you never saw RED; make sure it truly
  exercises the new behavior.
- Test is scoped wider than this task's interfaces → tighten it; drift breaks the
  contract the next phase inherits.

## Verifying the pass

Green on the one test is necessary, not sufficient. Before claiming done, hand
off to `drovr:verification-before-completion` — run the full suite and the build,
and confirm with evidence, not assertion.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for system/pacman.sh, the two pieces of system/deploy's host-package
# convergence whose logic is a model of something else's rules:
#
#   pacman_wants          -- the list format (comments, blanks, whitespace
#                            splitting) plus the per-host overlay, which decides
#                            what `pacman -S` is handed on each box;
#   pacman_ensure_include -- the one line appended to /etc/pacman.conf, a
#                            pacman-owned file we otherwise never touch. It must
#                            match whole lines (the stock config ships the same
#                            text commented out) and must never run twice.
#
# Both are sourced, not executed, so every case runs against the real functions
# in a temp tree. The privilege seam is SUDO: deploy leaves it at `sudo`, the
# cases set it empty so appends land in a temp file as the invoking user.
#
#   ./tests/system-packages.sh                  # tests ../system/pacman.sh
#   ./tests/system-packages.sh /path/to/pacman.sh
#
# Nothing here reads or writes /etc, and no case needs root.
set -u

LIB="${1:-$(dirname "$0")/../system/pacman.sh}"
[ -r "$LIB" ] || { echo "not readable: $LIB" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $LIB"
# shellcheck source=../system/pacman.sh
. "$LIB"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0
SUDO=

check() { # check <name> <expected> <actual>
  local name=$1 want=$2 got=$3
  n=$((n+1))
  if [ "$got" = "$want" ]; then
    printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$name"
  else
    printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n      want: [%s]\n      got:  [%s]\n' "$n" "$name" "$want" "$got"
    fails=$((fails+1))
  fi
}

# ── pacman_wants ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

mkdir -p "$D/pkgs"
cat > "$D/pkgs/packages" <<'EOF'
# a comment
btrfs-progs

zsh   # trailing comment
EOF

check "shared list: comments and blanks dropped" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" nosuchhost | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

cat > "$D/pkgs/packages.shiori" <<'EOF'
# host-only
steam
lib32-mesa
EOF

check "per-host overlay appends after the shared list" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh steam lib32-mesa" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" shiori | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

check "another host sees only the shared list" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" utsuho | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# The documented format is one package per line. Splitting on whitespace (rather
# than trusting the line) makes a two-names-on-one-line slip fail as two
# packages pacman reports as one missing each, not as one concatenated name that
# would silently never install.
printf 'a b\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.split"
check "two names on one line split into two" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh a b" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" split | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# A package named in both lists must reach pacman once: the "installing
# missing" line is read by a human, and -Qq would be asked twice for nothing.
printf 'zsh\nsteam\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.dup"
check "a name in both lists is emitted once" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh steam" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" dup | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

printf '# nothing but a comment\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.bare"
check "a comment-only host file adds nothing" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" bare | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# A host whose name would glob or traverse must not reach past the list dir.
check "host name is used literally, not as a pattern" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" '*' | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# Everything above is this repo's model of pacman.conf. This case asks pacman

# that pacman expands a glob in Include, and that a [multilib] section in an
# included file registers as a repo.

# nobody to ask.
if command -v pacman-conf >/dev/null && [ -r /etc/pacman.conf ]; then
  DROPIN="$(dirname "$LIB")/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf"
  mkdir -p "$D/conf.d"

  pacman_ensure_include "$D/real.conf" "Include = $D/conf.d/*.conf" >/dev/null

else

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.

Two forms:

The runless form keeps its artifacts in a run dir derived from the repo path and the task, which is what lets a resume find them — see `code_review::ephemeral_review_run`. system: per-host pacman lists, multilib as a drop-in, steam on shiori

Steam on Arch needs the multilib repo, which is off in the stock pacman.conf,
and it needs a 32-bit driver stack that no user profile can provide -- nixpkgs'
steam is an FHS env resolving GBM/DRI against NixOS paths, so on Arch it wants
nixGL, whose 32-bit half is the part that does not hold up. So this goes through
pacman. But system/packages reaches all four Arch hosts, and steam plus a
gigabyte of lib32 has no business on headless fujiwara.

Three pieces:

- system/packages.<host>, layered on the shared list by deploy and enforced the
  same way on every run. The shared list keeps its meaning ("must be present for
  this config to work", all hosts); the new one is per box. Only packages.shiori
  exists: steam, lib32-mesa, lib32-vulkan-intel, lib32-vulkan-icd-loader. The
  32-bit drivers are listed rather than left to steam's dependencies, because
  this file is the desired state and a driver that arrives as somebody else's
  dep leaves when they do.

- multilib as a repo file we own -- system/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf --
  reached by one glob Include appended to /etc/pacman.conf. Not an edit of that
  file and not a copy of it under etc/: it is pacman's own backup file, and
  owning a copy would turn pacman's changes to it into .pacnew nobody reads. One
  appended line survives that. The append is whole-line matched, because the
  stock config ships commented-out Include examples a substring match would read
  as "already enabled", and it leads with a newline, because an /etc file edited
  by hand may not end with one. Enabling a repo installs nothing, so this runs
  on all four hosts and the per-host list stays the only thing deciding what a
  box gets.

  The drop-in is installed by the multilib block itself rather than by the etc/
  copy further down, since that loop runs after `pacman -S` and an Include whose
  glob matches nothing is indistinguishable from multilib being off. That is the
  first time ordering against the etc/ copy has mattered, so the header comment
  claiming it does not is now accurate again.

- a warning, not a fix, when multilib has no sync db. Enabling a repo does not
  fetch one, and `pacman -S steam` against a repo with no db says "target not
  found", which reads as a typo in the list. deploy says the real thing and
  names `pacman -Syu`. It does not run `-Sy` itself: refreshing without
  upgrading is the partial-upgrade footgun the -S in the same block is careful
  to avoid.

The list format, the per-host overlay and the Include are now functions in
system/pacman.sh, sourced by deploy, so tests/system-packages.sh can drive them
against a temp tree through a SUDO seam. 21 cases, watched failing against empty
stubs first (15 of the 19 then-existing went red; the 4 that did not each have a
partner case pinning the other direction).

The last two cases stop modelling pacman and ask it: a copy of the host's real
/etc/pacman.conf plus the real drop-in, handed to pacman-conf, which answers
core extra -> core extra multilib with 425 mirrors resolved. That is the
assumption the whole design rests on -- that Include takes a glob, and that a
[multilib] section reached through one registers as a repo -- and it was checked
for falsifiability two ways: renaming the section to [multilibb] fails both
cases, and deleting the drop-in's own mirrorlist Include fails only the second.
Nothing in the suite writes to /etc or needs root.

install-base.sh deliberately still reads only the shared list: multilib is not
enabled in the live ISO's config for the target root, so pacstrapping steam
would fail the whole install. A rebuilt shiori picks it up on its first deploy.

Not yet applied on shiori -- the first deploy there will want `sudo pacman -Syu`
before it can resolve anything from multilib.

## Overview

**Evidence, not assertion.** Never declare a task done off your own judgment.

   actually exercise the behavior — a green line for a test that asserts nothing
   is not verification.

   skipped, say so plainly; do not imply coverage you don't have.

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/systematic-debugging

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**A fix you cannot explain is a guess wearing a diff.** Until the failure
happens on demand and you can say *mechanistically* why, any change you make is
as likely to hide the bug as to remove it. Follow the spirit, not the letter:
running the reproduction once, seeing red, and then fixing what you *assumed*
was wrong satisfies the ordering and proves nothing. The rule is that the cause
you fix is the cause you demonstrated.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** They will not have your hunch, your scrollback, or the shape you
recognized. They get the reproduction command, the cause you wrote down, and the
test you added — anything you only knew is lost at the phase boundary.

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIX BEFORE A REPRODUCTION AND A MECHANISTIC CAUSE.
```

No exceptions:

- **Do not act on a shape you recognize.** A failure matching one you have seen
  before is a reason to *suspect* a cause, not a reason to skip confirming it.
  Go read this instance's fixture, input, or state and confirm it is that bug.
  Recognition works on the assertion output; the bug lives somewhere you have
  not looked yet.
- **Do not read a conditional instruction as permission to skip its condition.**
  *"If it's the off-by-one, just fix it"* waives re-litigating the fix once the
  cause is confirmed — it never waives confirming it. Establish the antecedent
  yourself, then take the permission it grants.
- **Do not let a deadline shorten the verification.** After the fix, re-run the
  original trigger **and** the full suite — the scope
  `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick under time
  pressure. The clock does not change which tests can catch what this fix
  disturbed. If the full suite genuinely cannot be run here, name the exact
  command you did not run and do not report the bug as fixed.
- **Do not start fix #4.** Three *failed fixes* — the unit is defined in step 6 —
  means your model of the system is wrong, not that the fourth guess is due.
  Stop, say so, and question the design with whoever owns it before changing
  another line.
- **Do not substitute reasoning for a reproduction.** If you cannot trigger the
  failure on demand, that is the finding to report. Keep narrowing — smaller
  input, more logging, a read-only explorer — and stop before shipping a fix
  you cannot verify.

## Announce

Say this out loud when you start, before the first edit:

```
Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each bug you work, not once for the session. If you
fall back to `CHECKLIST.md` at a repo root, do not commit it.

1. **Reproduce.** Get a reliable, minimal trigger and record the exact command
   and its output. A bug you cannot reproduce on demand is a bug you cannot
   prove you fixed.
2. **Isolate.** Narrow to the smallest input, file, or code path that still
   shows it. Bisect, add logging, or dispatch a **read-only explorer** to map
   the suspect area. Fan-out investigation belongs to read-only explorers (e.g.
   `explore-mcp`), never to parallel writers — you keep the editing, which is
   what keeps drovr's single-writer rule intact.
3. **Root-cause.** Explain *why* it happens, mechanistically. "Adding this line
   makes it go away" is not a cause. Keep going until the explanation predicts
   the observed behavior exactly — including the parts you were not chasing.
4. **Fix.** Make the minimal change that addresses the cause, not the symptom.
5. **Verify.** Re-run your original trigger and confirm it is gone, then run the
   **full suite** — unconditionally, whatever the clock says.
   `drovr:verification-before-completion` owns what "full" means here and what
   evidence it takes; do not substitute a narrower scope you picked yourself.
   Add or fix a test that would have caught it.
6. **Escalate at three failed fixes.** A **failed fix** is one change you made,
   ran, and watched leave the failure in place. That is the unit — not edits, not
   builds, not ideas you considered and dropped. Count them for this one failure.
   At three, stop and question the design with whoever owns it; do not start fix
   #4 without that conversation. A run of wrong fixes is evidence about your
   model of the system, not about the next fix.

### The cycle

```dot
digraph debugging_loop {
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  repro  [label="reproduce it\non demand", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  story  [label="no trigger —\nyou have a story,\nnot a bug"];
  cause  [label="mechanistic cause", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  fix    [label="minimal fix,\nat the cause", fillcolor=palegreen];
  verify [label="trigger +\nthe full suite", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  stop   [label="three failed fixes —\nquestion the design", fillcolor=lightpink];
  // "failed fix" is procedure step 6's unit: a change made, run, and seen to
  // leave the failure in place.
  done   [label="fixed, with a test\nthat would have caught it"];

  repro  -> story  [label="cannot"];
  story  -> repro  [label="narrow: smaller input,\nlogging, read-only explorer"];
  repro  -> cause  [label="on demand"];
  cause  -> cause  [label="'it goes away' is\nnot a cause"];
  cause  -> fix    [label="predicts the\nobserved behavior"];
  fix    -> verify;
  verify -> done   [label="gone, suite green"];
  verify -> cause  [label="still failing —\ncount one failed fix"];
  verify -> stop   [label="that was the\nthird failed fix"];

```

## Red flags — STOP

Some of these are thoughts and some are things you have just observed. Either
way you are at the line, not past it — stop here and the loop is still intact.

- *"We've seen this exact failure before."* · *"They said if it's the off-by-one,
  just fix it."* · *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* — each of these
  opens a row in *Rationalizations* below. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are editing code and have not yet run the failing command yourself.* →
  Run it first. What you are fixing is a description of the bug, not the bug.
- *The failure went away and you cannot say why.* → Put the change back and
  confirm it returns. A fix whose mechanism you cannot state may be moving the
  bug rather than removing it.
- *The failure is intermittent, so you will "fix it and watch".* → You have no
  trigger, so you will have no proof. Narrow until it is on demand, or report
  that you could not.
- *You are about to start a fourth fix for the same failure.* → Stop. Three
  failed fixes is the escalation trigger, not a streak to break.
- **Any thought that ends with an edit landing before you can state the cause in
  one sentence.** The reason does not matter and the quality of the reasoning
  does not matter — if you are explaining why the cause can wait, that is the
  red flag.

## Rationalizations

The right-hand column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|

what does netrc do sorry

It's the credentials file curl/ftp invented, and nix reuses it: lines of `machine <host> login <user> password <secret>`.

Here it holds exactly one thing — the read token for your private attic binary cache at `attic.ko.ag/kube`. The nix daemon runs as root and you aren't a nix `trusted-user`, so the token has to reach it at system level. `system/deploy` decrypts `atticPullToken` from `secrets.yaml` and writes it to two places:

1. `/etc/determinate/netrc.custom` — Determinate Nix merges it into its own netrc via `/etc/determinate/config.json`.
2. `/etc/nix/netrc` — plain upstream nix's default `netrc-file`, for the hosts that aren't Determinate.

What it costs you when it's empty: nix gets a 401 from attic, treats the cache as unusable, and falls back to building. That's the whole point of `hms` waiting on CI — the switch is supposed to be a *download* of the closure the runner built. Without the token it's an hour of local compiling instead of a few minutes of transfer.

So the 0-byte `netrc.custom` isn't dangerous, just slow — and it's downstream of the missing GCP key, which `mise run bootstrap` restores.

Root-caused. The 404 is the only real failure in that output; the sudo line is a red herring.

**1. The sudo line is the exit trap, not the error.** `mise.toml`'s bootstrap registers cleanup on an EXIT trap on purpose ("a bootstrap that dies partway still retires the NOPASSWD sudo and sshd"). It runs `finalize-ssh.sh` under `sudo -n`, and shiori lost its NOPASSWD file long ago, so a dying task always prints that. Ignore it.

**2. Nothing got corrupted.** `set -euo pipefail` killed the task at the 404, before the `mv`. Confirmed on disk: `gcp-key.json.tmp` is 0 bytes, `gcp-key.json` still absent — so no empty key file was installed over anything.

**3. The 404 means the Secret genuinely isn't there.** Probed the endpoint unauthenticated:

```
GET https://k8s.ko.ag/version  -> 200
GET https://k8s.ko.ag/api      -> 403
```

That apiserver answers permission denials with **403**. So a **404** on `/api/v1/namespaces/bootstrap/secrets/sops-gcp-key` with a valid token is not "you can't see it" — it's "it isn't there". The `bootstrap` namespace or the `sops-gcp-key` Secret was never created, or has been deleted.

**Consequence: shiori cannot bootstrap itself.** The fetch path reads from a cluster Secret that has to be seeded *from a host that already holds the key* — `mise.toml:173` spells that out. There's no copy here to seed from.

So: which other machine still has `~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json`? On utsuho, setsuna or mari, this answers it in a second (and prints no secret):

```bash
ls -l ~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json
```

If one has it, seeding the cluster from there fixes every future host too. If none does, the fallback is minting a fresh service-account key in GCP for the `nix-key`/`host-key` KMS bindings — say the word and I'll look up exactly which SA and what it needs. Either way, don't paste the key contents in here.
